title: Medication Self-Administration Support
subtitle: For staff at Pennsylvania personal care homes and assisted living facilities. 55 Pa. Code 2600.65(f)(1) and 2800.65(i)(1).

eyebrow: The starting assumption, not the exception
title: How the model is supposed to work
points: Residents handle their own medications by default
Someone assesses whether that is safe, in writing
The assessment is revisited when things change
Those who cannot do it safely get it administered
Administering takes certification, not seniority

eyebrow: Two different jobs in one hallway
quote: Which job you are doing today has nothing to do with how long you have worked here.
attribution: Not how comfortable you feel, not how short-handed the building is. Only whether you hold the certification.

title: The check anybody can run, certified or not
Five things worth confirming out loud
points: Right resident — the name on the label
Right medication — what the label says
Right dose — how many, and how strong
Right time — and whether it is actually due
Right route — swallowed, dropped, inhaled, applied

quote: Moving a dose to later is a medication decision, and it is not yours.
attribution: Not early because you are going on break, not late because she is at lunch, not skipped because her stomach is off. Report it and let someone qualified decide.

title: Containers, labels, and the things that never happen

eyebrow: No exception, no emergency, no weekend
title: The absolute rules
points: Never move pills into a different container
Never give from an unlabeled bottle
Never use one resident's medication for another
Never carry two residents' medications at once
Never in your pocket, never left on a counter

quote: Some pills release a whole day's dose at once if you crush them.
attribution: Extended-release and enteric-coated tablets are built to come apart slowly. Crushing is a medication decision. Report the swallowing problem instead — it is solvable, usually by a different form.

title: Refusals, and the question worth asking

eyebrow: A refusal is a right, and usually a message
title: Why residents say no
points: It is making them nauseated
It is genuinely hard to swallow
They connected it to feeling dizzy — often correctly
Nobody ever told them what it is for
It is the one decision of the day still theirs

eyebrow: The kind thing that is a violation
quote: A pill hidden in applesauce is covert administration.
attribution: It removes a resident's right to refuse, and with a tablet that must not be crushed it is dangerous as well. Your job is not to solve the refusal. It is to report it.

title: What these medications actually do, and what to watch

eyebrow: You are not diagnosing — you are noticing
title: The common ones, and their tell
points: Blood thinners — bruising, and any head bump
Diabetes medication — shaky, sweaty, confused
Blood pressure medication — dizzy on standing
Opioids — drowsy, slowed breathing, constipation
Diuretics — dehydration, and urgent trips

quote: Sudden confusion in a resident on diabetes medication is a blood sugar until somebody proves otherwise.
attribution: Shaky, sweaty, pale, irritable, not making sense. This does not go in a note for the morning — it goes to a nurse now.

title: Everything that arrives from outside the building
What has to go through your process
points: Anything a family member brings in
Vitamins, herbals, and anything labeled natural
Sleep aids — a common wrong choice for elders
Antacids, laxatives, cough syrup, pain relievers
Medicated creams, drops, and patches

eyebrow: Even when she looks completely fine
quote: Do not wait to see whether anything happens.
attribution: Missed, doubled, wrong one, or a dose you have no record of — report it now. Somebody qualified makes that call, and they cannot make it if they do not know.

eyebrow: What to carry out of this course
quote: Almost no medication error here starts with carelessness. They start with somebody being kind.
attribution: Which is why the rule is not a judgment call. If you are not sure which side of the line you are standing on, you are outside it, and you ask.
